title: ABB launches Automation Extended program to modernize DCS without disrupting operations - Industrial Cyber
content:
ABB launches Automation Extended program to modernize DCS without disrupting operations
ABB has launched Automation Extended, a program designed to help industrial operators modernize distributed control systems without disrupting operations. The approach builds on ABB’s existing DCS platforms, allowing customers to protect prior investments while progressively introducing new automation capabilities.
The program is based on a modern, open, and modular automation architecture that supports advanced analytics, AI, and IoT integration. New technologies can be adopted at each customer’s pace, without exposing core operations to unnecessary risk. By separating core control functions from digital innovation layers, Automation Extended enables new capabilities to be deployed and scaled without interfering with mission-critical processes.
Industrial operations today face volatile markets, cybersecurity challenges, regulatory pressures and a rapidly changing workforce. ABB’s Automation Extended addresses these realities by enabling innovation with agility and pace without disruption to production, supporting advanced analytics and IoT integration, and simplifying operations for diverse skill levels.
Operators can continue to rely on trusted ABB systems such as ABB Ability System 800xA, ABB Ability Symphony Plus and ABB Freelance, while introducing technologies progressively and without operational interruption. This approach provides a structured, low-risk path to modernization, preserving continuity while enabling innovation.
“In industries we serve – many operating large and complex infrastructures that deliver essential resources – our customers rely on modernization without disruption,” said Peter Terwiesch, president of ABB’s Automation business area. “Automation Extended delivers exactly that: bringing future-ready capabilities into the systems they know and trust, with security and interoperability at the core.”
The Automation Extended program is implemented through a modern, open and modular environment designed for interoperability, scalability and seamless integration across industrial domains.
Based on separation of concerns principles, the automation ecosystem includes two distinct yet securely interconnected environments inclduing the control environment, a software‑defined domain that ensures robust, reliable and deterministic control for critical processes.
Secondly, the digital environment is securely connected to the control layer, enabling advanced applications, edge intelligence and real‑time analytics. This space leverages artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for decision support without disturbing proven control structures.
A single, unified and comprehensive automation service approach for ecosystem lifecycle management and optimization is applied for managing and maintaining these diverse technological environments.

title: Robotics Integration Is Transforming Global Surgical Care
content:
February 4, 2026
Robotic-assisted surgery represents one of the latest advances in surgical practice, offering advantages across specialties including urology, neurosurgery, gynecology, ophthalmology, traumatology, and orthopaedics, as well as cardiothoracic and general surgery.1
For certain procedures, when compared to laparoscopic and open surgery, robotic-assisted surgery is associated with reductions in recovery time, postoperative pain, complication rates, blood loss, and length of stay. This technology also allows for greater precision, dexterity, and visualization during procedures, which are particularly useful in complex cases such as those with dense adhesions and significant prior surgical history.
In addition, robotic-assisted surgery provides significant advantages for specific patient populations, such as those with obesity or complex anatomy, allowing for safer and more tailored interventions. From a surgeon’s perspective, robotics systems improve ergonomics and reduce physical fatigue during lengthy operations, positively impacting performance and surgical outcomes.
The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) highlights the importance of surgery as a component of universal health coverage (UHC)2 and advocates for strategies to strengthen surgical systems, including implementation of the National Surgical, Obstetric, and Anesthesia Plans. These comprehensive frameworks address gaps in surgical access, workforce training, infrastructure, and financing.
Evidence from LCoGS suggests that deficiencies in surgical, anesthetic, and obstetric (SAO) care contribute to 18 million preventable deaths annually.2 As robotic surgical systems evolve, their integration into healthcare infrastructure may align with global efforts to strengthen surgical systems and capacity while reducing disparity in access to quality care.
Robotic assistance has been applied across various surgical subspecialties. In 1985, the first surgical robot, the Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly 560 (PUMA 560), was used in neurosurgery for a biopsy procedure.
In urology, robotics platforms are primarily used for laparoscopic radical and partial prostatectomy in the treatment of prostate cancer, as well as for nephrectomy and lymphadenectomy procedures. In orthopaedic surgery, total hip arthroplasty was the first robotic procedure performed, followed by knee arthroplasty. Studies have shown that robotic assistance in orthopaedics improves alignment, facilitates limb lengthening, and enhances patient satisfaction. Fracture fixation in trauma surgery represents a substantial potential for future robotics innovation.
In gynecology, robotics systems are widely used for procedures such as hysterectomies and myomectomies. While in the area of otolaryngology, applications are generally categorized into retro-auricular hairline incisions and transoral robotic surgery, depending on the pathology.
The field of cardiac surgery also has seen growing use of robotics platforms, particularly for minimally invasive procedures such as endoscopic coronary artery bypass grafting and mitral valve repair. One of the earliest robotic cardiac procedures included the closure of an atrial septal defect.
While vascular surgeons are beginning to explore robotic assistance, its use remains off label in the US, and broader application in this specialty is still in the early stages of development. Specialized robotics platforms also have been developed for spinal, ophthalmic, and other nonabdominal surgeries. These platforms continue to evolve, offering various capabilities designed to improve microsurgical precision while maintaining safety and reproducibility.
Initially approved solely for the purpose of visualization and retraction, the da Vinci system became the first to receive US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for general surgery in 2000.3 To demonstrate its safety, 300 robotic-assisted surgeries were performed in Europe, beginning with a robotic-assisted cholecystectomy in Belgium in 1997.4
Today, robotic-assisted surgery accounts for 5% of surgeries in the US, 2% in Europe, and less than 1% in the rest of the world, correlating with the proportion of each region’s gross domestic product spent on healthcare.5 In 2005, a robotic-assisted cystectomy was performed in Egypt, and robotic surgery for achalasia cardia was performed in Argentina, which was the first procedure of its kind performed in the region. India and China were among the first Asian countries to adopt robotic surgery in 2006, with other countries, including Japan, Pakistan, and Indonesia following suit in 2009, 2011, and 2012, respectively. Robotic surgery has gradually spread across the former Soviet states since the 2000s, with Russia adopting the technology in 2007, Poland in 2010, and Kazakhstan in 2018.
In comparison, robotic surgery has seen less adoption in Latin America and Africa. Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela have had incremental adoption of this technology, while in Africa, robotic surgery has only been reported in Egypt, South Africa, and Tunisia.
Recently, newer robotics platforms have been developed in China, Germany, India, Italy, South Korea, Switzerland, and the UK.3 Although most of these platforms are approved only by local regulatory bodies, their availability is expected to reduce costs and promote further integration of robotics into surgical practice. The development and adoption of robotics systems have been limited in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where public health priorities often focus on infectious diseases, maternal health, and trauma. Robotic surgery is typically concentrated in private or urban healthcare facilities, exacerbating existing disparities.
From a global health perspective, robotic-assisted surgery aligns with key health priorities, such as the third aim outlined in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, which emphasizes good health and well-being and supports efforts to improve access to safe, high-quality surgical care.2 Robotic surgery can contribute to achieving UHC by increasing access to advanced surgical interventions and reducing perioperative morbidity and mortality.
While the initial investment and operational costs of robotic surgery are substantial, often due to longer OR times and higher equipment-related expenses, some studies suggest that the long-term benefits, such as reduced postoperative complications, shorter hospital stays, and quicker return to work may offset these costs and support overall health system sustainability.6 However, evidence remains mixed and further research is needed to determine whether these benefits translate to low hospitalization costs for patients. For more information on the cost of robotic surgery, see the cover story in this issue, “Cost of Robotic Surgery Remains Complex Equation.”
Robotic surgery necessitates specialized training and continued practice for surgeons, anesthesiologists, nurses, OR staff, and technical teams. Notably, many LMICs face a shortage of a skilled surgical workforce, not limited to robotic surgery. LCoGS has set a target of achieving a minimum SAO density of 20 per 100,000 population by 2030 for adequate access to surgical care. More than 808,000 SAO healthcare providers need to be trained by 2030 to reach this density.2 It is critical to first develop an adequate surgical workforce that provides essential, safe, comprehensive care to support training in minimally invasive surgery.
Following the development of an adequate surgical workforce, future hurdles include a lack of structured fellowships, mentorship, and exposure to minimally invasive surgical techniques. This diminished exposure contributes to the continuing gap in implementing robotic surgery programs. Fortunately, middle-income countries in Latin America and India are developing solutions to the unique hurdles healthcare systems face in resource-limited settings. Brazil has 2,500 da Vinci-trained surgeons and a national accreditation program due to industry partnerships, while surgeons practicing in India may seek out robotic surgery fellowships through a philanthropic platform, the Vattikuti Foundation.
Virtual reality (VR) surgical training and remote-controlled robotics systems are technological solutions that may address some of these training-related hurdles. The Eyesi surgical simulator is a VR training platform that is intended to accelerate surgeon proficiency and reduce operative times. Remote-control systems show promise in expanding access to surgical care and supervised robotic surgery training in underserved regions, potentially reducing travel-related logistical and financial burdens.
Additional challenges impeding enhanced adoption of this technology include infrastructure gaps, high costs, and a lack of institutional support. An estimated $1 million–$1.5 million is necessary to implement a robotic platform in the US, with expenditures averaging $4,000 per procedure.6 These costs encompass the initial purchase, maintenance, and the supply of specialized instruments. Individual institutions routinely bear the financial burden owing to a lack of government funding.
Insurance coverage can also hinder widespread adoption. For instance, while robotic-assisted surgery was introduced in Japan in 2009, many procedures were not covered until 2018.7
A prevalent barrier for many healthcare facilities in LMICs and rural settings within high- income countries (HICs) is the inconsistency in basic infrastructural elements, such as reliable power supply, advanced imaging facilities, and high-speed internet connectivity for potential telemedicine applications, posing significant constraints for adopting a unified robotic surgical system and training. Health policy initiatives and industry collaboration may ease some of these challenges.
In many LMICs and rural HICs, access to the technical support necessary to implement and maintain robotics systems is limited. For example, the first robotic surgery platform in Pakistan was rendered dysfunctional soon after installation until an improved platform was installed 2 years later.8
Data regarding quality control, cost-effectiveness, and overall outcomes in LMICs are lacking, and extrapolation from the HIC data may not be appropriate for this setting. Addressing these technological gaps is crucial for successfully adopting robotic surgery in these settings.
The European Union, the FDA, and Japan classify robotics systems as medical devices. At the same time, in other countries, such as Indonesia, this technology is unregulated with healthcare institutions making decisions without legal directives from the government. Regulatory bodies may approve robotic surgery systems, but their application and prerequisite training are left to surgeons, healthcare institutions, and manufacturers.
While the companies that manufacture these devices provide some quality assurance and benefits for approved uses, robotics systems are also used for unapproved indications. Policymakers in several industrialized nations seek to implement more stringent oversight of emerging technology, especially given its increasing autonomous capabilities. Autonomous surgical robots have demonstrated proficiency in phlebotomy, bowel anastomosis, and knee replacement surgery, among other procedures.9 These applications remain in the experimental phase for now but risks to patient safety and other concerns must be considered to preempt misuse.
One proposal is to define six levels of autonomy to distinguish various categories of medical devices and establish unique risks and, thereby, regulations required for each. Another consideration is requiring specialized robotics training for surgeons before performing robotic surgery on patients. As surgical robots continue to reside within a legal and regulatory gray area, the benefits and drawbacks of additional regulations that may hinder scientific advancement are unclear.
Historically, surgery has been significantly underfunded within the broader context of global health, receiving limited attention compared to other health concerns such as maternal and child health and infectious diseases.
A significant step was taken in 2020, when policymakers directed the US Agency for International Development (USAID) funding toward global surgery programs, signaling a financial commitment to addressing surgical disparities and responding to a growing public health need. This move reflects a pivotal shift in funding priorities and firmly establishes surgery as a key component of global health agendas.
However, comprehensive estimates of these financial investments are challenging to quantify, as funding allocations often flow through multiple channels. A systematic analysis indicated that multilateral organizations like the World Health Organization and USAID collectively disbursed approximately 31% of total health development assistance worldwide, including nonsurgical disciplines.10 Shifting funding priorities may lead to significant impact on the accessibility of surgical services, and could hinder innovative advancements, including broader access to robotic surgery platforms.
Emerging technologies hold significant promise in making robotic surgery more accessible, particularly in LMICs and rural areas.
Efforts are underway to develop more affordable and modular robotics systems, such as India’s locally developed SSi Mantra platform, explicitly designed to reduce acquisition and operational costs compared with existing platforms.3 Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into robotic surgical systems, such as the SSi Mantra platform, offers opportunities to support intraoperative decision-making, precision, and overall surgical performance, ultimately aiming to reduce complications and improve patient outcomes. AI-driven algorithms can support surgeons by providing real-time analytics and guidance, which is valuable in resource-constrained settings.
Telesurgery and remote tele-proctoring technologies offer promising solutions to bridge geographical and logistical barriers by enabling experienced surgeons to operate remotely and mentor and train surgeons with limited robotics experience, thereby extending robotic surgical expertise to underserved regions. However, successfully implementing this technology requires robust telecommunication networks, stable sources of electricity, and technical support to realize their full potential. These innovations represent advancements toward achieving equitable, scalable, high-quality surgical care worldwide.
Equitable access remains a significant concern worldwide as robotics systems are predominantly concentrated in high-income, urban settings, widening the global healthcare gap. Bridging this divide requires intentional efforts in equitable distribution of this technology and expanded infrastructure development. Health systems also must critically assess the cost-effectiveness of robotics platforms, as their high acquisition and maintenance costs may not be justifiable in all contexts.
In deciding between robotic-assisted surgery and conventional surgical options, patient autonomy and informed consent are important considerations. Patients should be informed about the nature of robotic assistance, including potential risks, benefits, alternatives, and the surgeon’s experience, to ensure ethical, transparent, and patient-centered care. Misconceptions regarding robotic surgery should be clarified, as many patients may mistakenly assume this approach to be superior to traditional surgical approaches in all indications.
Financial incentives may encourage inappropriate use of robotic surgery in instances where it is not indicated and offers minimal advantages. Prioritizing the acquisition of robotics systems in regions without access to laparoscopic surgery and other vital resources may represent an inappropriate use of financial resources, leading to suboptimal patient outcomes. Ethical and sustainable adoption of robotics systems requires evaluation of local needs and capabilities to ensure this technology serves patients and does not come at the cost of broader surgical access.
Robotic-assisted surgery is an advancement in modern medicine and minimally invasive surgery, offering improved surgical precision, patient outcomes, and ergonomics. However, global implementation and adoption remain variable, with significant infrastructure, training, and funding barriers, especially in low-resource settings. Efforts to close these gaps through capacity building, regulatory frameworks, and emerging technologies such as AI and telesurgery may address some of these barriers. Investment in robotic surgery in the global surgery context must be considered in light of existing unmet needs to ensure optimal population-level outcomes.
Dr. Kaiser Sadiq is a preliminary general surgery resident at The George Washington University in Washington, DC, and is Vice-Chair of the ACS Resident and Associate Society Membership Workgroup.
Dr. Surmai Shukla is an Institutional National Research Service Award (T32)-funded postdoctoral fellow at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in Pennsylvania.

title: Robot Orders Grow 6.6% in 2025 as General Industries Drive Broader Automation Adoption
content:
News
Robot Orders Grow 6.6% in 2025 as General Industries Drive Broader Automation Adoption
ANN ARBOR, Michigan – North American robot orders rose in 2025, reflecting strong investment in automation across a growing range of industries. According to new data from the Association for Advancing Automation (A3), companies across the region ordered 36,766 robots valued at $2.25 billion last year. Compared to 2024, this represents a 6.6% increase in units ordered and a 10.1% increase in revenue1.
General Industry Drives Market Gains in 2025
Robot demand from non-automotive customers outpaced demand from their automotive industry counterparts in 2025, with general industries capturing the majority share of units ordered throughout the year. Industries such as food and consumer goods, semiconductors and electronics, and life sciences all contributed to this broad-based momentum. While automotive component orders remained below 2024 levels, activity from automotive OEMs showed meaningful improvement. This uptick from major vehicle manufacturers may signal stabilization in core automotive markets heading into 2026.
Strong Finish to the Year in Q4
In the fourth quarter of 2025, companies ordered 10,325 robots valued at $579 million. These figures represent a 6.6% increase in units and an 8.7% rise in revenue compared to Q4 2024, using adjusted comparisons from matched reporting companies. This marks the sixth consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth and lifted annual totals to their highest level since 2022.
Collaborative Robots Accelerate in Q4, End Year at Nearly 20% Share
Collaborative robots continued their upward trajectory, accounting for 28.6% of all robots ordered in Q4 2025 and 14.7% of quarterly revenue. This represents 2,953 units valued at $85 million, the highest quarterly volume recorded since A3 began reporting collaborative robot as a distinct category in Q1 2025.
Across the full year, collaborative robot orders totaled 7,212 units valued at $241 million. This represents 19.6% of total robots ordered in 2025 and 10.7% of total revenue, underscoring the growing importance of collaborative systems as part of modern automation strategies.
Automation Momentum Expected to Continue into 2026
“The rebound in robot orders over the course of 2025 reflects renewed confidence in automation as a long-term solution to competitive pressures,” said Alex Shikany, Executive Vice President at A3. “We’re seeing increasing adoption across sectors, especially in general industry applications and at automotive OEMs, as manufacturers look to automation to address workforce shortages, manage reshoring initiatives, and boost productivity.”
Shikany also pointed to the significance of Q4 trends. “Automotive OEMs came back strong in the second half of the year, which often serves as a leading indicator for growth in supplier and component markets. Combined with steady demand across food, electronics, and other non-automotive industries, this points to a positive outlook for 2026.”
More detailed market breakouts and graphs for Q4 and full-year 2025 are available upon request for press and within the A3 Vault for member companies. For deeper insights, A3 members can subscribe to MI+, the Association’s premium market intelligence platform, featuring forecasts, dashboards, and in-depth reporting to support better decision-making.

Discover the latest in robotics, vision, AI, motion control, and more at Automate 2026, North America’s largest automation showcase, taking place June 22–25 in Chicago. This year’s show will be bigger than ever, with A3’s popular Humanoid Robot Forum co-located with Automate (June 23-24) and a dedicated Humanoid Robot Pavilion sponsored by NVIDIA premiering on the Automate show floor.
Registration for both events is now open at www.automate.org.

title: Insect-inspired adaptive behavioral compensation strategy against olfactory sensory deficiency for robotic odor source localization - npj Robotics
content:
Abstract
The ability to navigate toward potential mates, food sources, or nesting sites is a fundamental trait shared across species. Despite their small nervous systems, insects demonstrate remarkable odor-guided navigation, making them ideal models for bioinspired robotics. Although robots capable of odor-source localization have been developed, their practical deployment remains limited, particularly under conditions involving physical impairment. In this study, we investigated how sensory deficits affect odor localization behavior in male silk moth Bombyx mori, which locates females using sex pheromones. Remarkably, even after the removal of one antenna, the primary olfactory organ, the silk moth retained its ability to locate the odor source. Behavioral analyses revealed that navigational strategy depended on the spatial position of odor detection. We replicated this strategy in a quadrupedal robot by designing a system capable of estimating odor positions analogous to moth antennae. Robotic experiments confirmed that adaptive behavioral selection based on bilateral or unilateral odor cues sustains efficient odor localization. These findings highlight fundamental principles of robust robotic navigation system development capable of maintaining performance even under sensor impairment, as required for long-duration or rescue missions.
Similar content being viewed by others
Introduction
Numerous organisms, ranging from small insects to mammals, can navigate to specific locations in search of potential mates, feeding grounds, and nesting sites. This navigational trait contributes considerably to survival and prosperity. Many species use airborne chemicals or odors as one of their key cues for navigation1,2. Moreover, owing to their persistence and diffusivity, odors serve as an effective means of communication, allowing information transmission through chemicals dispersed spatially in the air. However, odor distribution can be unpredictable both temporally and spatially and is influenced by factors, such as wind and physical obstacles that may obstruct odorous chemical transmission3,4,5. Nevertheless, by effectively processing the acquired information, organisms can efficiently utilize odors to inform and modulate their behavior accordingly.
A notable advantage of olfactory navigation is its ability to facilitate exploration and identification, particularly in scenarios where visual detection is impractical. For example, dogs rely heavily on olfaction for search and identification tasks, using their heightened sense of smell to locate victims in disaster situations and detect hazardous materials or narcotics at airports and event venues6. However, not all dogs possess this ability, and considerable time and resources are required for training7. Additionally, the olfactory sensitivity of an animal may diminish over time due to habituation, and navigating life-threatening environments presents a challenge for these animals. Although olfactory navigation is a significant area of inquiry, it depends heavily on the olfactory abilities of animals. Consequently, numerous attempts have been made to address the challenges of olfactory navigation by developing robotic systems8,9,10,11. Various insect-inspired approaches have been proposed to replicate the real-time search behaviors of insects and implement these behaviors in robotic designs12,13,14,15. These approaches work effectively in environments with stable odors. However, when these algorithms are implemented on a robot and their search performance is evaluated in outdoor environments, where unforeseen conditions are likely to occur, their limitations become apparent. In particular, the search strategy of moving upwind in response to odor stimuli has been proven ineffective16. This is because in natural outdoor settings, the directions of odor plumes and wind do not necessarily coincide4; thus, even if the estimation of wind direction functions accurately, the odor source may not be located upwind. Under such circumstances, a search strategy relying primarily on olfactory information to track the odor is effective. However, these systems typically mimic insect behavior in response to olfactory stimuli, resulting in limited adaptability and robustness to physical changes in the robotic body.
To address this issue, efforts have been made to enhance the search performance of robots by measuring electromyography and neural activity in the brain and by conducting accurate and quantitative analyses of behavioral modulation mechanisms, rather than solely imitating the relationship between odor stimuli and behavioral responses17,18. Moreover, methods have been proposed to improve the performance of odor source localization by integrating additional sensory information, such as wind and visual stimuli with olfactory cues16,19,20. Although these innovations have successfully increased adaptability to environmental changes, discussions on the robustness of robotic systems in the face of physical alterations remain insufficient. In practice, the body of a robot may degrade during extended operations or while navigating through debris-laden environments. Particularly concerning is how to adjust behavior when sensors, particularly the sensory organs used for odor detection, cease to function efficiently. This is critical for the practical application of odor-source-sensing robots. Most insect-inspired algorithms designed for odor-source searching have been developed under the assumption that bilateral odor information is accessible. Consequently, the performance of odor-source localization is likely to decline significantly when a robot relies solely on unilateral odor information.
Behavioral studies on insects indicate that cockroaches can still locate odor sources even after the loss of an antenna, their primary olfactory sensory organ21,22. This capacity arises from odors, particularly pheromone information, detected at various positions along the antenna, which are encoded by distinct projecting neurons that allow a single antenna to acquire spatial information23. Similarly, hawkmoths have been used to determine the direction of an odor source using only one antenna24. These findings suggest that elucidating how insects with relatively simple nervous systems adapt their behavior following the loss of an antenna may yield insights into enhancing the robustness of robotic systems in response to physical changes. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the adaptive behavioral strategies that insects use when a part of their sensory organs is lost and to replicate these strategies through engineering. Specifically, we investigated the behavior of adult male silk moths that demonstrate female localization behavior in response to sex pheromones and measured changes in their behavior following the removal of an antenna. Based on our results, we modeled the relationship between odor reception and behavioral selection in the context of a single antenna and implemented this model in a quadrupedal robot to evaluate the feasibility of artificially recreating this function.
Results
Based on the research concept shown in Fig. 1, this study aimed to analyze the adaptive behavioral selection process associated with the loss of a sensory organ in adult male silk moths and to replicate this process artificially. To this end, we conducted behavioral and robotic experiments using silk moths.
Changes in odor source localization performance associated with sensory organ loss
The capacity of male silk moths to localize a female was assessed through a free-walking experiment using intact individuals and individuals in which the left antenna had been ablated (Non-Left-Antenna, NLA). NLA individuals were ablated, after an odor source-localization experiment in intact individuals, and were used 1 h after ablation. The odor source was set as the origin, and the localization experiment was performed 15 cm from the odor source. Localization was considered successful if the moth approached the odor source within 1 min.
As shown in Fig. 2A–C, the results of the odor source-localization experiment were analyzed in terms of localization success rate, localization time, and tortuosity. They indicated no significant decline in localization performance, even in cases of sensory organ deficiency (Fisher’s exact test, p < 0.05, N = 20). The indices of localization time and tortuosity indicated that sensory organ loss caused the moths to move along a route that took longer to localize (Welch’s t-test, p < 0.05). In addition, the NLA increased the tendency of rotational movements compared to the intact condition. To visualize this strategy, we represented all the trajectories for each individual condition as a migration pathway ratio map (Fig. 2D, E), which revealed that in the intact condition, the silk moths moved along an undeviating route, whereas when only a single antenna was present (NLA condition), the trajectory was biased toward the remaining antenna. To depict this clearly in Fig. 2F, we present a graph comparing the typical trajectories for each individual condition. Black and red lines on the graph represent intact and NLA individuals, respectively. In the intact state, silk moths move linearly toward the odor source, whereas the route taken by NLA individuals is characterized by an initial rotational movement commencing the search, followed by a subsequent approach to the odor source via the right-side route (y in the positive direction). Thus, these results indicate that even if an antenna is missing, silk moths retain the capacity to acquire sufficient odor information, which facilitates the localization of an odor source based on the selection of a route skewed toward the remaining antenna.
Changes in the behavioral decision-making process induced by sensory organ loss
The results of the free-walking experiment described in the previous section revealed that, even if an antenna is lost, the ability to localize the odor source can be maintained using the remaining antenna. Based on these findings, we analyzed the behavioral selection process associated with antennal loss in detail. To perform a highly accurate analysis of behavior in response to odor stimuli, we analyzed the head movement, which has been established to be highly correlated with movement direction25,26.
According to the results of previous studies, the moth performs sharp rotational movements as its heading angle increases25. The condition in which the head of the moth faces forward is defined as a head angle of 0 rad, with the left and right directions designated negative and positive, respectively. A negative head angle corresponds to a moth moving to the left, whereas a positive head angle indicates movement to the right. As described in the previous section, intact and NLA individuals were used in this study. To simulate increases in the strength of the odor stimulus when the source of the odor is approached, the stimulus was presented to the silk moth with gradually increased frequency from 0.1 to 1 Hz in 0.03-Hz increments (see supplemental video S2). The odor stimulus-presentation pattern was determined under the condition of the odor stimulus release from the left and right odor outlets.
The experimental data, classified based on the rotational direction in response to the left and right odor stimuli, are shown in Fig. 3 (N = 10). Each column in Fig. 3 represents the current direction of movement when the moth received the stimulus (1st column, left direction; 2nd column, right direction), whereas each row indicates the direction from which the stimulus was presented (1st row, stimulus from the left; 2nd row, stimulus from the right). Figure 3 illustrates the frequency at which the moth selected a particular direction of movement between receiving the current odor stimulus and the subsequent one using a probability density function (PDF). For instance, if the PDF is high for negative direction, it indicates that the moth predominantly chooses to move to the left until the next odor stimulus is received. Figure 3 shows the direction of the odor stimulus and the direction in which the silk moth moved. The black and red lines in Fig. 3 represent the intact and NLA conditions, respectively, the horizontal axis represents the left/right head orientations, and the vertical axis represents the frequency. The PDF for right rotation was similar regardless of the direction of the odor stimulus, indicating that the silk moth rotated to the right more frequently than to the left, although it rotated slightly to the left. These observations were similar for both intact individuals and those which underwent antennal removal. In contrast, in the case of left rotation toward the side of the removed antenna, in which the odor stimulus was received from the left side, there is a similar tendency to right rotation, whereas when the stimulus was received from the right side, there is a difference in the selected direction of rotation. In the case of intact individuals, regardless of whether the odor stimulus was received from the left or right, rotation tended to be in the same direction as that of the stimulus, whereas when the antenna was removed, rotation also occurred in the direction of the side of removal. Accordingly, we found that, as a consequence of antennal loss, behavioral selection is modified such that if an odor is detected at the base, emphasis is placed on rotating to the same side, whereas if the odor is detected at the tip of the antenna, behavioral selection is characterized by a comprehensive search of both the same and opposite sides.
To summarize, antennal loss leads to two simple outcomes depending on the current direction of rotation and the spatial position of antennal odor detection, as shown in Fig. 3.
- 
                    1.
                    
                      If the odor is detected at the base of the antenna, a PDF that favors further rotation to the same side is taken.
- 
                    2.
                    
                      If the odor is detected at the tip of the antenna, a two-peak PDF that has a slightly higher frequency on the opposite side is taken.
Changes in the behavioral selection process due to antennal loss can contribute to maintaining the odor source-localization capacity of silk moths.
Verification experiment using a robot
We experimentally evaluated whether changes in the behavioral selection process due to antennal loss, observed in biological experiments, were effective for odor source localization. When a silk moth loses its antenna, it changes its next action depending on its current direction of movement and the part of the antenna that detects the odor. In this robotic experiment, we reconstructed the essential elements of the decision-making process in a robotic framework to examine the validity and effectiveness of the search strategy. Based on the biological experimental results, we constructed a behavioral selection algorithm for odor source localization. For convenience, we refer to the proposed algorithm as the context-dependent moth-inspired (CDMI) odor-source localization algorithm. This algorithm was developed based on the SZL (surge-zigzag-loop) algorithm17, which emulates the fundamental search behavior elicited by silk moths. Flowcharts of both the SZL and CDMI algorithms are presented in Fig. 4. These algorithms consist of two primary states, a “Surge” state, triggered by the detection of odor stimuli, and a “Zigzag/Loop” state, which emerges upon the loss of odor information. A detailed explanation of the algorithm is provided in the Section “Odor source localization algorithm”. The proposed CDMI and control SZL algorithms were incorporated in the robot. In addition, we established two conditions for the odor-sensing device of the robot, a group with both left- and right-side odor-sensing devices intact and a group with only the right odor-sensing device intact, simulating sensory organ loss (NLA). In verification experiments conducted in an indoor environment, we comprehensively covered all possible conditions to investigate the relationship between the state of the antenna and search algorithm. Each experiment was repeated 10 times.
The results obtained for the search success rate, search time, and tortuosity in the indoor experiments are shown in Fig. 5A–C, where the gray and red shadings represent the SZL and CDMI, respectively. For the intact group, we recorded search success rates of 100% for the SZL algorithm, but only 40% for CDMI algorithm. The location time was rapid for the SZL, and with this algorithm, the robot was able to localize the odor source with less meandering than earlier. In contrast, for the NLA group, robots incorporating the CDMI algorithm had a search success rate of 80%, which was higher than that obtained using the SZL algorithm. Accordingly, we sought to determine factors contributing to the higher success rate of the CDMI algorithm, which accounts for the odor position by comparing search trajectories. Figure 5D shows the trajectories of the robot in the intact and NLA groups. The robot trajectories were created for the intact case that used the SZL algorithm and NLA case that used the CDMI algorithm. The black lines in Fig. 5D represent the intact condition, the red lines represent sensory organ defects, and the blue lines represent areas with a high probability of odor presence (odor edge). Comparing the trajectories, in intact antenna condition, we found that both the silk moth (Fig. 2F) and robot (Fig. 5D) approached the odor source in a linear manner without deviating from the blue region. Conversely, when either an antenna or an odor-sensing device was missing, both the moths (Fig. 2F) and robot (Fig. 5D) entered and exited the blue region and showed a pattern of movement that followed the odor edge. To compare this quantitatively, we counted the number of times the silk moth and robot passed over the blue dashed line, which represents the edge of the odor, from their trajectories. The results are shown in Table 1. The results in Table 1 show that the number of times the edge was passed increased significantly, owing to antenna loss.
Notably, given that this edge zone is characterized by marked changes in odor information, we speculate that when bilateral information is unavailable, it may be possible to approach the odor source by selecting a location in which substantial spatial changes in odor information are present. Accordingly, when bilateral information is available, moth behavior may be dependent on the timing of odor detection on the left and right sides, whereas when this information is no longer available, the behavior is determined based on the spatial position detection of the remaining antenna, thereby facilitating the maintenance of odor source localization.
Having assessed the performance of the robot in an indoor setting, we sought to experimentally verify whether this behavioral selection was equally applicable in a less predictable external environment. The purpose of this outdoor field experiment was to determine whether it is preferable to use the timing of odor detection under intact sensory conditions and the spatial position detection of the odor under sensory-deficient conditions. To this end, we incorporated the SZL algorithm into an intact robot and the CDMI algorithm in a defective robot; each experiment was conducted 10 times. We found that even in a highly unpredictable outdoor environment, the search success rate was 80% for both conditions (Fig. 6A). Figure 6B, C shows that the search time and meandering rate were shorter when both the NLA and CDMI algorithms were used in the field experiment, and the robot moved in a shorter time with less meandering than earlier. Since the distribution of odors is discrete in open air, the strategy of following the odor edge may likely lead to the odor source. This observation indicates that adjusting the behavioral selection process to a specific situation confers the robot a function that maintains constant search performance.
Discussion
In this study, we investigated the adaptability of an insect to a circumstance in which sensory organs necessary for odor source location was lost and attempted to reconstruct the adaptability mechanism in a robot. The insect used in this study was an adult male silk moth that could locate a female based on the detection of specific sex pheromones released by a female. The capacity of odor source location of moths, including silk moths, is a particularly well-researched area, not only in terms of their behavior but also in terms of the mechanisms underlying odor information processing in the brain27,28,29. Certain moths can accurately pinpoint the location of females, even over considerable distances of ≦4 km30. If this impressive ability can be artificially reproduced, robots with heightened olfactory capacities can be developed.
Previously, researchers assumed that the odor-localization capacity of moths was enhanced by odor sensors (antennas) located on both the left and right sides of the head31, enabling spatially oriented movement toward an odor source by simultaneously detecting odors at spatially distant locations. However, in fast-moving flying insects, movement speed may exceed the brain’s capacity to process left-right odor asymmetry and make behavioral decisions accordingly. Therefore, directional information can be acquired using other modalities32,33. In an experiment with a flying insect Heliothis virescens, one antenna was removed, as in this study, and the odor source localization was assessed34. Results of the study revealed that even in fast-moving flying insects, the search performance decreased, but the odor source localization function was not completely lost. Additionally, similar to our findings in the present study, these antennal-ablated H. virescens moths approached the odor source with a trajectory characterized by in-and-out movement of the odor edge.
In contrast, silk moths, which move slower than other flying insects, change direction in response to asymmetric odor stimuli35,36. A distinctive characteristic of the silk moth is its heightened sensitivity to pheromonal stimuli, which exhibits a well-defined female-localization behavior. This behavior is modulated according to the strength of the wind stimuli when the insect is exposed to a steady airflow37,38. However, silk moths do not exhibit anemotactic behavior, i.e., movement toward the upwind direction in response to wind stimuli33. Consequently, olfactory stimulation plays an important role in silk moths. Previous studies have investigated the temporal processing of odor information by silk moths in response to intermittent odor stimuli35,39. For example, a study investigating the temporal integration of odor stimuli using optogenetic GAL4/UAS transgenic silk moths expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) demonstrated that when odor inputs were delivered to the same antenna within approximately 80 ms, they were temporally integrated, whereas intermittently presented odors with intervals > 80 ms were perceived as distinct stimulus events39. In addition, previous behavioral experiments examining how silk moths utilize bilateral olfactory information have shown that, when odor stimuli are presented separately to the left and right antennae with a temporal delay, silk moths tend to move toward the side that receives the odor the latter (approximately 50 ms later)35. This finding suggests that, despite their relatively slow locomotion, silk moths can independently evaluate asymmetric olfactory inputs from both sides and make behavioral decisions based on this information. Collectively, these findings indicate that even odor stimuli arriving within extremely brief temporal windows can be discriminated as separate inputs, and that silk moths possess the capacity to determine their direction of movement based on bilateral olfactory cues. However, the search strategy adopted by these moths in response to antennal loss, which prevents assessment of the timing of odor detection on the left and right sides, remains unclear. With a single remaining antenna, moths can use odor information processing through temporal integration40. This process of making behavioral decisions, which is based on the utilization of differences in information such as body direction and position at a certain time of odor detection, and the information gained on subsequent detection of the same odor, bears a close resemblance to short-term memory and corresponds to spatial sampling associated with movement. Investigating this temporal integration is of particular interest. However, determining the physiological areas, which control the memory of silk moths and support this temporal integration mechanism, is challenging. In addition, the attempt to incorporate the temporal integration process into a multilegged robot may fail if the odometry information is inaccurate41. Consequently, we speculate that an algorithm that modifies the behavioral selection according to the spatial position detection of the antenna when a single antenna is used can provide more robust functionality. However, deriving evidence for biological hypotheses based on the results obtained from silk moth behavioral experiments and validating it using robots requires in-depth genetic and physiological analyses, which can be considered a limitation of the present study.
Notably, the proposed algorithm, CDMI, exhibited superior search performance in outdoor environments compared with indoor conditions under NLA conditions. From the perspective of “embodiment”, this observation suggests that the body, including its sensory organs, functions more than a mere input–output apparatus42. Although it is often assumed that the brain solely generates motor outputs for adaptive behavior, the classical literature on embodiment43 emphasizes that adaptive behavior emerges not only from neural processes but also from continuous interactions between the body and its surrounding environment. In this view, the brain’s role is not to “command” but rather to catalyze the formation of behavioral patterns through such interactions. Moreover, in the process of acquiring signals from the environment and converting them into behavior, two essential functions are involved, sensory pre-processing and motor post-processing. A canonical example of sensory pre-processing can be found in crickets, whose auditory organs are located on their legs. Internal air passages within their bodies create phase differences in the incoming sounds, potentially allowing them to estimate the direction of the sound source44,45. In other words, the body filters and amplifies environmental information before it reaches the nervous system. A well-known example of motor post-processing is that muscles and tendons do not simply transmit neural signals as they are; instead, they act as filters that preferentially pass only low-frequency components. Thus, the output of the brain is effectively reconstructed using the structural properties of the body. Our experimental results can be interpreted as a manifestation of such “sensory preprocessing”, wherein physical embodiment plays a crucial role in shaping behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, the framework used in this study, implementing biological insights into robotic systems and empirically validating their functions, aligns with the concept of “biorobotics”, which advocates the use of robots as models to explain animal behavior42. Unlike computational simulations, which cannot fully capture the physical constraints, sensory noise, frictional forces, and environmental uncertainties encountered by living organisms, real-world robotic implementations provide a tangible means of verification. Simulations that constitute an exceptionally powerful tool for evaluating the validity of models derived from the results of biological experiments, as well as for identifying unknown parameters inherent within those models, need to be emphasized. However, if how such models function in the real world is the objective, then robots can serve as an effective means for understanding biological intelligence. By iteratively cycling biological experimentation and robotic modeling, we can achieve mutual advancement, gaining deeper insights into biological mechanisms while enhancing the adaptability and robustness of robotic systems. This integrative framework holds great promise in advancing biology and engineering46.
The understanding of the adaptive and robust architecture of insect intelligence will contribute significantly to the future establishment of “insect-inspired artificial intelligence (AI)” systems47,48,49. With the rapid advancement in computational power, a trend toward enhancing robotic autonomy and adaptability through deep learning frameworks, most notably transformer-based models is growing. However, owing to their structural characteristics, transformers do not have strong “inductive biases”, which grants them high flexibility in learning but simultaneously necessitates vast amounts of training data. Consequently, providing comprehensive datasets encompassing all real-world phenomena is not feasible. Moreover, training these models requires considerable computational resources, energy, and time. Robots that rely solely on these learning-based architectures may face severe functional limitations in emergency or disaster scenarios where sufficient energy supply and global communication cannot be guaranteed. Under these constrained conditions, robots must demonstrate heightened autonomy, robustness, and adaptability. In this context, “insect-inspired artificial intelligence (AI)”, which seeks to integrate the intelligent functionalities observed in insects into robotic systems, presents a promising alternative50. As mentioned above, designing insect-inspired AI also involves establishing a methodology that can effectively deal with complex, changing environments by devising sensors and body structures from the perspective of “embodied intelligence”. This will allow us to dramatically improve the autonomy and adaptability of robots in the future by coevolving both modular and structural AI inspired by biological intelligence, rather than relying solely on transformers.
However, our study had some limitations, which is important to establish appropriate future research directions. Given that we focused on behavioral changes resulting from antennal loss, the assessments of the behavioral changes in response to olfactory stimuli was limited. Even in OSL experiments using robots, evaluating the performance under conditions that simulate physical antennal loss from an intact state is not yet possible. This limitation is caused by the physical arrangement of the array of odor sensors to the microcontroller via wires, thereby preventing automatic disconnections during the experiments. In future work, by modularizing and wirelessly enabling an odor-sensing device, we plan to investigate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm during the transition from an intact system to the system with simulated antennal loss. The modularization and wireless integration of odor-sensing devices also allow for immediate and straightforward replacement in the event of malfunction, representing a promising step toward practical implementation. Because flying insects also utilize other sensory modalities to make behavioral decisions, it is reasonable to assume that silk moths bearing a single antenna might enhance their search performance by integrating information obtained from other types of sensory input. Moreover, when designing robots, the incorporation of sensory modalities other than odor detection is required for wide-area, three-dimensional searching. Adopting such a multimodality framework is inevitable for developing practical odor-source-localization robots, and future research should be focused on identifying the combinations of modalities that enhance search performance when sensory organ loss occurs.
Methods
Study animal
Silk moths (Bombyx mori; Lepidoptera: Bombycidae) were purchased from Ehime Sansyu Co. (Ehime, Japan). To reduce their activity, adult male silk moths were cooled to 16 °C the day following eclosion and tested within 2–6 days of eclosion. Prior to conducting the behavioral experiments, the silk moths were maintained at room temperature (24–28 °C) for at least 10 min.
Upon becoming an adult, the silk moth exhibited little spontaneous locomotor activity; however, when the silk moth detected a female sex pheromone, it elicited female-searching behavior51,52,53. The direction of movement during this searching behavior was determined by the timing or concentration of odor detection between the left and right antennae35. Furthermore, although silk moths do not exhibit anemotaxis behavior observed in cockroaches and flying moths54, where they move upwind when detecting an odor, the behavior of silk moths is modulated by multimodal information from the odor and wind.
Dissection scissors were used to excise the antennae from the base, ensuring that no part remained on the head. To attach a fixture to the silk moth and tether a measurement system, the back of the moth was exposed to a cotton swab moistened with water. The fixture was then attached using an adhesive (G17; KONISHI Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan) that did not influence the behavior of the silk moths55. The fixture was fabricated using a 3D printer (Onyx, Markforge Holding Corporation, MA, USA).
Free-walking experimental field
A free-walking experiment using silk moths was conducted in a laboratory at 24 °C, in an open space without obstacles that could impede odor transmission. A pheromone cartridge containing 1000 ng bombykol ((E,Z)-10,12-hexadecadien-1-ol), the sex pheromone released by female silk moths, was used as the odor source. The pheromone cartridge consisted of a circular disc cut from filter paper (Filter Paper 5A; ADVANTEC, Tokyo, Japan) with a diameter of approximately 10 mm. To facilitate pheromone diffusion, the cartridge was placed in a glass pipe and air was pumped through it. Compressed air from an air compressor (NIP30L, Nihon Denko, Aichi, Japan) was passed through three gas-washing bottles containing degreased cotton, activated carbon, and water and was adjusted to 1.0 L/min using a flow meter (KZ-7002–05A; AS ONE CORPORATION, Osaka, Japan). The stimulation timing was controlled by switching the flow path of the solenoid valve (VT307; SMC Corporation, Tokyo, Japan). The odor emission frequency was set to 1 Hz (duration, 0.2 s; interval, 0.8 s), which is a value close to the pheromone emission of female silk moths56. The silk moth modulates its behavior in response to wind stimuli exceeding 1.0 m/s37. Therefore, free-walking experiments were conducted under wind velocities below 1.0 m/s, where the influence of wind stimuli is minimal and behavioral modulation is likely to occur solely in response to olfactory cues. The environmental wind in the experimental field was generated by a fan (YLS-18; Yamazen Corporation, Osaka, Japan) to approximately 0.6 m/s, thereby facilitating the diffusion of the odorant.
To prevent pheromone residue in the experimental field, the floor was wiped with ethanol after each trial and ventilated for >30 min. Before the subsequent trial, a silk moth was placed in the experimental field to verify that the residual pheromones did not elicit female localization behavior. Therefore, we reset the experimental field for each trial.
Tethered behavioral experiment device
A tethered behavior measurement device was constructed based on a previous study using an insect VR system38. This device uses a 60-mm diameter styrene foam sphere levitated by a small fan that enables the insect to actively rotate the sphere. The extent of sphere rotation is generally considered to reflect the amount of insect movement, and behavioral changes were analyzed. However, this method of behavioral measurement requires the sphere to move widely, complicating subtle behavioral change measurement. Therefore, we installed a camera (C910; Logitech Co. Ltd., Lausanne, Switzerland) on top of the device to record the movement of the silk moth head. A high correlation between the direction of movement and the direction of the head of the silk moth has been reported25,26. Consequently, by analyzing head movements, we can accurately determine the direction where the silk moth moves. Odor stimuli were presented to the left and right antennae of the silk moth from an oblique front (15 °angle), as shown in Fig. 7. The odor stimulus used was 1000 ng bombykol ((E,Z)-10,12-hexadecadien-1-ol). The odor stimulus apparatus used was the same as described in the “Free-walking experimental field” section. In the experiments conducted using a tethered behavioral device, the airflow associated with odor stimulation was carefully controlled to prevent the silk moth from misinterpreting the stimulus as a mechanosensory cue. Following a previous study35, the airflow rate was set to a low value of 0.5 L/min. We confirmed prior to the experiment that air at this flow rate did not move the antennae. To focus on measuring behavioral changes in response to odor stimuli, we did not provide any wind stimuli.
Quadruped odor source searching robot system
The robot incorporating in the search algorithm was a quadrupedal robot (Unitree Go1; Unitree, Hangzhou, China), as shown in Fig. 8A. The configuration diagram of this system is shown in Fig. 8B. The quadrupedal robot platform can move even on slightly uneven ground; therefore, the same system was used for the localization experiment in both indoor and outdoor settings. The high-level control mode, which utilizes a stable walking pattern built into Unitree Go1 (Company, City, Country), was used to control the robot. In this mode, the robot can move toward the desired direction by sending the movement speed in the translational and rotational directions to Unitree Go1 via UDP communication. As the robot was intended to operate completely autonomously, a small PC (NucBox G2; GMKtec, Shenzhen, China) was installed on the robot, and signal processing and localization algorithms for the additional odor sensor were incorporated. As the PC lacked a port for reading analog values, the values of each odor sensor were acquired via a small microcontroller (ESP32; Espressif Systems Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China), with information between the PC and microcontroller being exchanged via serial communication. The robot was equipped with an odor-sensing device that functioned in a manner similar to that of an antenna. Insect antennae comprise multiple olfactory receptors that are difficult to replicate accurately. However, we designed an odor-sensing device that can be used to reproduce the functions of an insect antenna by determining the position of the antenna at which an odor is detected. Odor source localization algorithm
The algorithm for odor source localization incorporated into the robot was created based on female localization behavior of the target insect (male silk moths), as shown in Fig. 4A17. When a moth responds to an odor stimulus, it moves in a straight line toward odor direction, which is referred to as a surge, for approximately 0.5 s, it then changes the direction by rotating left and right to detect the next odor, before finally rotating in one direction (zigzag/loop). Silk moth moves in a loop state after three zigzag actions as it switches the direction of rotation three times in average53. This is generally referred to as the SZL algorithm, as these three behavioral states are switched by turning odor stimuli on and off. As shown in Fig. 4B, the direction of the surge in the conventional SZL algorithm is determined by the timing of the odor detection by the left and right antennae. For example, when an odor is received by the left antenna, the robot moves diagonally in a straight line to the left side. After the surge, the robot transitioned to a zigzag state, with the initial direction of rotation is the opposite to the direction of surge movement. Therefore, if a surge is performed diagonally to the left, the initial zigzag rotation direction is to the right. From the perspective of the robot’s motion performance, the translational and angular velocities were set to 0.2 m/s and 0.6 rad/s, respectively.
In contrast, under conditions in which the silk moth has lost an antenna, although the behavior selection algorithm according to the odor detection position has the same three basic behavioral states (surge, zigzag, and loop) as the SZL algorithm, the behavior is determined by the PDF obtained from biological experiments. As shown in Fig. 4C, depending on the current rotational direction and odor detection position, the direction of the surge movement was determined from the PDF corresponding to each situation. This PDF is identical to that obtained from the silk moth experiment. In this context, two types of PDF exist, those for the intact state (indicated by the black line) and those for antennal loss (indicated by the red line). In the presence of odor-sensing devices on both the left and right sides, a black PDF was used, and when only a single odor-sensing device (antennal loss) was present, a red PDF was used. For convenience, in this study, we refer to an algorithms in which actions were determined based on the odor-detection position and PDF as CDMI. Based on the selected PDF, a point is randomly sampled from the distribution according to the probability. Given that the horizontal axis of the PDF represents a value corresponding to the strength of rotation, when the sampling point is Pr, the angular velocity ω changes according to the condition in Eq. 5 depending on the value of Pr.
Experimental environment for robotic odor source localization
The evaluation experiments using the robot were conducted in indoor and outdoor test areas, as shown in Fig. 9, both of which are open spaces with no obstacles. Ethanol (used as an odor source for safety and availability reasons) was volatilized by placing it in a gas wash bottle into which 10 L/min of air was flown. A wind source, set to 1.0 and 2.0 m/s indoors and outdoors, respectively, was placed behind the odor source to promote odor diffusion. The temperature, humidity, and natural wind speed on the day of the outdoor experiment were approximately 8 °C, 32%, and 4 m/s, respectively.
Using the odor source as the origin, an experiment with the robot was conducted from a distance of approximately 3 m. To prevent the robot from accidentally succeeding in localizing the source by simply moving in a straight line, the initial posture of the robot was tilted 45° toward the odor source. The movements of the robot were observed using an external camera (GoPro HERO11 Black; GoPro Inc., CA, USA). In the indoor environment, regular ventilation was provided to prevent ethanol from filling the room.

In outdoor robotic experiments, camera images were analyzed using projective transformation and converted into video images that were calibrated for accurate distances. The data obtained from the biological and robotic experiments were analyzed using the numerical analysis software MATLAB version 2023b (MathWorks, MA, USA). A MATLAB analysis program was self-coded.

title: Robot Ready: The U.S. Needs a National Robotics Strategy Now - AUVSI

Robot Ready: The U.S. Needs a National Robotics Strategy Now
February 11, 2026
The age of autonomy and advanced robotics is here, and dominance in this industry will determine who leads the next industrial revolution. This is not hyperbole: AI-powered robotics are already transforming entire sectors, reshaping factories, supply chains, infrastructure, and defense, and creating new economic and strategic landscapes. The United States must be prepared to compete.
That urgency is why AUVSI, together with a coalition of policymakers and industry leaders, recently launched the bipartisan Partnership for Robotics Competitiveness (PfRC), an initiative to advance federal policy and a National Robotics Strategy to secure U.S. leadership in robotics and physical AI.
The U.S. must successfully deploy robotics at scale to secure higher productivity, a stronger industrial base, and greater resilience, and to ensure the robotics industry delivers good jobs, enhanced safety, and lasting prosperity. Otherwise, America risks dependence on foreign technology, exposure to PRC leverage and supply-chain shocks, and weaker global competitiveness.
Why the Partnership for Robotics Competitivenessâand a National StrategyâMatter Now
The U.S. leads the world in robotics innovation, but without a coherent national framework, that advantage cannot be fully realized. Federal policy is fragmented, procurement pathways are inconsistent, and issues like workforce readiness, liability, and safety are often addressed reactively. Meanwhile, global competitors are advancing coordinated, state-backed strategies that align industrial policy, supply chains, workforce development, and government demand to accelerate adoption at scale. The result is a growing gap between U.S. technological leadership and deployment.
The PfRC exists to close that gap. It frames robotics and autonomy as strategic infrastructure, emphasizing coordination over prescription and ensuring federal policy supports secure supply chains, workforce readiness, responsible deployment, and long-term competitiveness. With investment in advanced robotics surging and policymakers increasingly focused on national security, industrial resilience, and global competition, there has never been a more critical moment to act.
XPONENTIAL: A Forum for Shaping the Future of Robotics
A national robotics strategy must be informed by real-world developments. AUVSIâs XPONENTIAL 2026 conference this May will convene policymakers, industry leaders, and technologists to explore the challenges and opportunities shaping robotics, autonomy, and uncrewed systems.
With participants from more than 20 industries and 60 countries, over 550 exhibitors, and hands-on demonstrations spanning mobility, defense, infrastructure, energy, and public safety, XPONENTIAL provides a snapshot of how robotics is reshaping the economy and national security that can help guide a national strategy. Key sessions focused on actionable insights include:
- Robotics Policy in the 21st Century: How federal policy can support innovation, strengthen supply chains, and advance national security.
- Moving Targets: Navigating evolving procurement and funding mechanisms to accelerate adoption in government and industry.
- Guardrails for Innovation: Managing operational, legal, and cybersecurity risk without slowing progress.
- Adventures in Human-Robot Teaming: How collaboration between humans and robots is transforming industrial workflows and workforce requirements.
XPONENTIAL provides stakeholders a space to surface challenges, share insights, and explore decisions that will shape U.S. leadership in robotics and autonomy. AUVSIâs new robotics white paper outlines PfRCâs vision for a National Robotics Strategy and provides a roadmap for policymakers and industry, while the conference will be a forum to test, debate, expand, and refine those ideas in real time.
The Path Forward
Robotics and physical AI will define the next era of U.S. economic and national security leadership. Success depends not just on innovation but on the ability to deploy, scale, and sustain these technologies responsibly, and that requires coordinated action across government, industry, and academia.
The Partnership for Robotics Competitiveness provides the policy framework to align innovation with deployment. XPONENTIAL brings together the leaders responsible for making that alignment real.
The time to act is now: the U.S. must get Robot Ready.
Contact Grant Baker to learn more about joining the PfRC.

title: Is China Leading the Robotics Revolution? | ChinaPower Project
